edits.old: Apply this formula to $F=|s|^2e^{-mv}$, with the value on the pole set immaterial. It proves equality of the possibly infinite integrals. Finiteness characterizes the multiplier-ideal section spaces, so it proves the asserted isometry without needing an extension theorem for sections. An orthonormal basis therefore pulls back to an orthonormal basis, which proves the kernel identities. Finally, a nonnegative function on the base is bounded if and only if its pullback is bounded, proving the statement about bounded weighted sections and their multiplication.

edits.old: Apply \cref{thm:kn-continuous}, whose proof was given in \cref{chap:weak-equations}, to the Hermitian manifold $(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma)$. It gives a continuous $v$ and a positive scalar $a$ with $(\sigma+\ddc v)^{n-1}=af\sigma^{n-1}$. Since $\sigma$ is closed, bounded Stokes gives $a\int f\sigma^{n-1}=1$. Thus $a=c/(2n)$ and $v$ solves the required base equation. Bounded $\sigma$-plurisubharmonic functions are in the full-mass class of the reference potential $0$. The measure $(f/\int f\sigma^{n-1})\sigma^{n-1}$ has mass one and charges no pluripolar set. The normalized uniqueness theorem for that class in \cite[theorem on the relative Monge--Amp\`ere equation]{SGPT} gives uniqueness of $v$ up to constants. Consequently \eqref{eq:hopf-reduced-equation} has a continuous solution unique up to constants within the descended class. For smooth positive $f$, \cref{thm:tw-smooth} on the same base gives smooth $v$, with the same scalar fixed by Stokes. Existence and regularity here use the proofs already supplied in this book; only the stated closed-class uniqueness is imported from \cite{SGPT}.
edits.new: Since $\sigma$ is closed, it satisfies the Guan--Li condition. Apply \cref{uni-thm:GL-intro} to $(\mathbb P^{n-1},\sigma)$. It gives a continuous base solution with the scalar just computed, unique up to constants among bounded $\sigma$-plurisubharmonic functions. Consequently \eqref{eq:hopf-reduced-equation} has a continuous solution unique up to constants within the descended class. For smooth positive $f$, \cref{thm:tw-smooth} on the same base gives smooth $v$, with the same scalar fixed by Stokes. Both existence and uniqueness therefore follow from results proved earlier in this book.

edits.old: At a positive threshold and in dimension at least two, \cref{thm:semipositive-dual-exact-equation} allows a smooth semipositive maximizer that is strictly positive outside a proper analytic set $Z$. It gives the exact global equation, smoothness off $Z$, and uniqueness of all threshold subsolutions modulo constants. The uniqueness proof takes the maximum of two subsolutions and uses a Gauduchon integral to remove the resulting nonpositive divisorial difference. It requires no prescribed singularity type. The classes of the positive pole divisors are then linearly independent by \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-divisor-independence}. Moreover, \cref{prop:semipositive-dual-exponential-limit} proves whole-family normalized $L^1$ convergence of the exponential solutions, with a fixed lower barrier and $b\leq c_\lambda\leq b\mathrm{e}^{C\lambda}$. If the threshold solution also admits a genuine smaller-background envelope, \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-capacity-limit} strengthens this to capacity convergence. Whether that extra condition is automatic, and global regularity across $Z$, remain open here.

\subsection{A branched projective example}

A smooth semipositive maximizer need not be strictly positive, even when the threshold solution is smooth. The following example also shows why smoothness of the density root was asserted only off the degeneracy set.

\begin{example}\label{ex:semipositive-projective-maximizer}
For every $n\geq2$, there is a smooth nonnegative density $f$ on $\mathbb P^n$, vanishing precisely on the coordinate hyperplanes, such that $b_\omega(f)=1$ and $D_{f^{1/n}}$ has a smooth semipositive maximizer strictly positive off those hyperplanes. Here $\omega$ is the Fubini--Study form, normalized by $\int_{\mathbb P^n}\omega^n=1$, and $\mathrm{d}V=\omega^n$. The threshold solution is smooth, but $f^{1/n}$ is not differentiable at a general point of any coordinate hyperplane. There is no smooth strictly positive maximizing form. The normalized greatest exponential solutions converge uniformly to the normalized threshold solution.
\end{example}
\begin{proof}
Let
\[
 F[Z_0:\cdots:Z_n]=[Z_0^2:\cdots:Z_n^2],\qquad
 A=\tfrac12F^*\omega.
\]
The homogeneous formula
\[
 u=\tfrac12\log\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^n|Z_i|^4\right)
       -\log\!\left(\sum_{i=0}^n|Z_i|^2\right)
\]
defines a smooth function on projective space, and $A=\omega+\ddc u$. This form is semipositive and is strictly positive exactly where every homogeneous coordinate is nonzero. Define
\[
 f=A^n/\omega^n,\qquad T=A^{n-1}.
\]
Closed Stokes gives $\int f\omega^n=\int\omega\wedge T=1$. Thus $T\in\mathscr G_\omega$. Every genuine $\omega$-plurisubharmonic potential has extended mass at most one: each bounded truncation has mass one, and restriction away from its truncation level can only decrease that mass. Consequently an inequality $\mathrm{MA}^{\mathrm{ext}}_\omega(v)\geq c f\omega^n$ forces $c\leq1$. The smooth solution $u$ gives the reverse bound, so $b_\omega(f)=1$.

The determinant formula for smooth semipositive forms gives
\[
 k_T=f^{(n-1)/n},\qquad
 D_{f^{1/n}}(T)=\int_{\mathbb P^n}f\omega^n=1.
\]
By \eqref{eq:integrable-current-supremum} and $\rho_\omega(f^{1/n})=b_\omega(f)^{-1/n}=1$, this is a maximizer. Its strict positivity away from the coordinate hyperplanes follows from that of $A$; on a hyperplane $A$ has deficient rank, and so does its cofactor matrix.

For the density root, use the chart $Z_0=1$ with coordinates $z_1,\ldots,z_n$. Pulling back the Fubini--Study volume by $(z_1,\ldots,z_n)\mapsto(z_1^2,\ldots,z_n^2)$ and including the factor $2^{-n}$ gives
\[
 f(z)=2^n\left(\prod_{i=1}^n|z_i|^2\right)
       \frac{(1+\sum_i|z_i|^2)^{n+1}}
            {(1+\sum_i|z_i|^4)^{n+1}}.
\]
Near a point of $\{z_1=0\}$ with all the other coordinates nonzero, its $n$th root is $|z_1|^{2/n}$ times a smooth strictly positive function. Restriction to a real line transverse to that hyperplane proves nondifferentiability, including the absolute-value case $n=2$. Coordinate symmetry gives the same conclusion on every component. The absence of a smooth strictly positive maximizer follows from \cref{cor:kahler-smooth-dual-attainment}, since $f$ has zeros. Finally $f$ is bounded, so \cref{cor:semipositive-dual-lp-limit} gives the uniform exponential limit.
\end{proof}
